1.

sentences.text: 1 the purported direction contained therein eliminating the provisions of Section 5A of the said Act, being Annexure K thereof and/or the said  2 purported notice being Annexure L, were ultra vires the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

A direction was also sought upon the respondents to withdraw,
revoke, recall and/or cancel the impugned notification and the purported direction contained therein.

2. The present application being GA 4 of 2022 was filed by the Defence Estate Officer, Kolkata Circle, inter alia, praying for addition of several parties as indicated in paragraph 17 of the said application as respondents in the said writ petition.
3. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the applicant for addition of parties submitted as follows.
The Defence Estate Officer, Kolkata Circle filed the application for addition of parties in respect of the present writ petition.
The writ petition was filed challenging a notification under Section 4 under the Land Acquisition Act whereby the land being 19, River Side Road within the B Cantonment was sought to be acquired.
Admittedly the property in B Cantonment belonged to the Government of India and was governed under the Grants Act, 1895.
It was comprised of an Old Grant Bungalow under the said General Order of the Governor General in Council no. 179 dated 12.09.1836 wherein conditions of land in occupation were laid down.

Regulation 6 stated that no ground would be granted except on the conditions as laid down in the Regulations which were to be subscribed by every grantee as well as those to whom the grant might be subsequently transferred.
From a careful reading of Sections 2 and 3 of the Government Grants Act, 1895, it would be evident that the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 was not applicable to the government grants.
It was pertinent to mention that as per the General Land Register, the Holder of Occupancy Rights of the property in question was in the name of Messers Hukumchand Jute Mills Ltd.
The Deed of Indenture dated 17.05.1949 was executed by one John Frank Snaith in favour of the Hukumchand Jute Mills Ltd.
By a letter dated 01.12.1948 the transfer was sanctioned by the Government of India.
After such transfer, no further sale or transfer of the property was sanction/approved by the Government of India.
Therefore, the petitioner's right to maintain the writ petition was in serious doubt.

By an order dated 03.02.2022, this Court directed the State respondents to take instructions regarding whether the land in question could be returned to the petitioner on payment of compensation or whether the State respondents were agreeable to purchase the land directly from the petitioners at the market rate.
By an order dated 17.02.2002, the learned Judge passed an order granting last chance to the State respondents to take instructions.

Two separate appeals were preferred against the aforesaid orders and by a common order dated 07.03.2022, the Division Bench held that no final decision had been arrived at by the learned Single Bench and the learned Single Judge was requested to consider all submissions.
The application for addition of parties was filed on the apprehension that an adverse order could be passed against the Union of India in its absence.

sentences.text: authorities mentioned in paragraph 17 of the application were necessary parties and ought to have been impleaded from the very inception.
The writ petitioner and or their alleged predecessor in interest very well knew that they were not the absolute owners of the property.
Nor they had any right to transfer the same.
They never thought it fit to inform the Central Government about the requisition of the property or the subsequent acquisition proceeding initiated by the State Government.
In none of the litigations it was pointed out by the writ petitioners that the property belonged to the Central Government.
It was a case of conscious suppression of material fact.
The nature of an Old Grant property was such that the Government was the absolute owner with the power of resumption.
Correspondences were purportedly made between the Government of India and the Government of West Bengal regarding the acquisition by the State in respect of the property.
The contention of the writ petitioner in opposing the prayer for addition of the parties that the title to the land had no bearing on the adjudication of any issue was not tenable at all.
Paragraph (1) and prayer (b) of the writ petitioner belied such proposition.
In order to challenge the acquisition proceeding, the petitioner would necessarily have to establish that it had a right in the property in question.
In the present case the writ petitioner had no right, title or interest in the property in question.
The holder of occupancy right did not have any right to collect compensation in respect of the property from the State Government without the permission of the Central Government.
Besides, the writ petition related to acquisition property in question of which the Union of India was the undisputed owner.
Therefore, the Union of India was a necessary party in deciding such writ.

Reliance was placed on Union of India Versus Dinshaw Shapoorjij Ankleswari & Ors. reported in (2014) 14 SCC 204 on the explanation of the status of Old Grant Property, the overriding effect of the Government Grants Act, 1895 and also its scope and extent.

entities.text: Union of India Versus Dinshaw Shapoorjij Ankleswari & Ors. reported in (2014) 14 SCC 204
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Reliance was also placed on Repaka Bhyravamurthy & Anr. V. Mudippi Venkatraju & Ors. AIR 2002 AP 77 on the point that a person might not be entitled to be impleaded as a party only for the purpose of enhancement of the compensation, but if any other question arose that touched upon the issue of entitlement or apportionment of the amount of compensation, the same might be considered by reason of an application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC.

entities.text: Repaka Bhyravamurthy & Anr. V. Mudippi Venkatraju & Ors. AIR 2002 AP 77
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: As regards the decisions relied upon by the writ petitioners, in Tractor Farm Equipment Ltd. V. Secretary to the Government of Assam reported at AIR Gauhati 73 it was held that the scope of Order 1 Rule 10 in a civil suit and a writ petition were different.

entities.text: Tractor Farm Equipment Ltd. V. Secretary to the Government of Assam reported at AIR Gauhati 73
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In a writ petition the Court also had to take into account the consequences or effects that the decision would have on the interest of others.
The judgment of Gurmeet Singh Bhatia Versus Kiran Kant Robinson reported at (2020) 13 SCC 773 was distinguishable as it was passed in a suit for specific performance.

entities.text: Gurmeet Singh Bhatia Versus Kiran Kant Robinson reported at (2020) 13 SCC 773
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The decision in Union of India Versus Bharti Airtel Limited reported at (2022) 4 SCC 328 laid down a ratio that would rather help the writ petitioner.

entities.text: Union of India Versus Bharti Airtel Limited reported at (2022) 4 SCC 328
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, the application for addition of party should be allowed in the facts of the present case and in the interest of justice.
4. Learned senior counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted as follows.
The land in question being Premises no. 19, River Side Road, Barrackpore, District - North 24 Parganas, West Bengal, purportedly belonged to the Union of India represented by the Ministry of Defence.

The said land was handed over to the writ petitioners for construction of structures and the terms of such grant were governed by the General Order passed by the Governor General in Counsel no. 179 dated 12.09.1836.
Simply because the land in question belonged to the Union of India, Ministry of Defence, it need not be made a party respondent.

The present writ petition was filed challenging the Orient Paper & Industries Ltd vs State Of West Bengal & Ors on 16 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45956339/
3 actions of the State Government in passing notification dated 29.12.1994 and the subsequent notice dated 31.03.1995, thereby invoking the emergency provisions under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act and dispensing with mandatory requirement of compliance of the provisions of Section 5A of the said Act.

sentences.text: Among other things, reliefs were sought that the impugned notification and the purported notice be declared ultra vires the 1894 Act.
The provisions of Section 5A of the said Act required the State Government to invite objections from the stakeholders prior to acquisitioning a land.
By trying to bypass the mandatory provisions without sufficient reason, the State Government had acted arbitrarily.
For the purpose of determining the above questions, it was not necessary to hear the contentions of the Central Government.
The writ petitioner being the dominus litis, was the master of the proceeding and hence, his choice of parties in the writ proceedings should be given preference to.
It was the petitioner's choice to initiate the proceeding against the State respondents and therefore, at its disapproval, a third party should not be impleaded in the proceeding.
On this, reliance was placed on Gurmeet Singh Bhatia Versus Kiran Kant Robinson, (2020) 13 SCC 773.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Moreover, no action of the Central Government authorities were challenged in the present writ petition and as such, they were not necessary parties.
On this, reliance was placed on Union of India Versus Bharti Airtel Limited and Ors, 2022 4 SCC 328.

sentences.text: On the other hand, the decisions relied upon on behalf of the applicant were clearly distinguishable from the present facts.

In Union of India and another Versus Dinshaw Shapoorjij Ankleswari & Ors. (supra),
the land in question was resumed by the Central Government.

sentences.text: In Repaka Bhyravamurthy's Case (supra), the Hon'ble Court only held that if any other question arose that touched the issue of entitlement or apportionment of the amount of compensation, the same might be considered by reason of an application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC.

The decision in Tractor Farm Equipment Ltd., Chennai Vs Secretary to the Government of Assam (supra) in fact came more to the aid of the contentions of the writ petitioners and was hardly of any help to the applicant.

sentences.text:
In the case at hand,
no relief was claimed against the Central Government authorities.
Nor were the reliefs claimed in the writ petition capable of affecting in any manner the interest of the Central Government.
Therefore, the application filed on behalf of the Central Government for addition of the Central Government and its officers as parties was liable to be dismissed.

5. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State submitted that the prime relief sought by the writ petitioner was against the State Authorities and the State Authorities were prepared to deal with the same.
6. I heard the submission of learned counsels for the parties and perused the writ petition, the application and the written notes of submissions.

7. It is an admitted position that the property in question i.e., 19 Riverside Road, Barrackpore, North 24 Parganas falls within the Barrackpore Cantonment, which, in turn, belonged to the Government of India and was governed under the Grants Act, 1895.

8. The writ petitioner contented that they were the Holder of Occupancy Rights of the property in question and have filed the writ petition seeking certain relief against the State in respect of the land acquisition in question.

Therefore, the applicants need not be added as respondent or be heard in the writ petition as neither any relief has been sought against the Central Government nor the reliefs Orient Paper & Industries Ltd vs State Of West Bengal & Ors on 16 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/45956339/
4 sought against the State Government could affect adversely the rights of the Central Government.

sentences.text: 9. On the other hand, the applicants have raised certain important issues.
According to them, the property in question comprised of an Old Grant Bungalow under the General Order of the Governor General in Council no. 1 dated 12.09.1836.
From a careful reading of Sections 2 and 3 of the Government Grants Act, 1895, it would be clear that the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 did not apply to the Government grants.

Regulation 6 provided that no ground would be granted except on the conditions as laid down in the Regulations that were to be subscribed by every grantee as well as those to whom the grant might be subsequently transferred.
Pertinently, as per the General Land Register, the Holder of Occupancy Rights of the property in question was in the name of one Messers Hukumchand Jute Mills Ltd.
By a letter dated 01.12.1948, the transfer dated 17.05.1949 was sanctioned by the Government of India.
But, no further sale or transfer of the property was sanctioned or approved by the Government of India after that.
Therefore, the petitioner's right to maintain the writ petition was itself in doubt.
It is further germane to mention that the writ petitioners did not inform the Central Government about all the proceedings that went on in respect of the present lis.
The petitioners knew that they were not the absolute owners of property and had no right to transfer the same.

According to the applicants, the writ petitioners did not have any right, title or interest in the property in question and therefore, did not have any right to collect compensation in respect of the property from the State Government without the permission of the Central Government.
10. It appears that the property is indeed governed by the Government Grants Act, 1895.
It is also evident that the property in question belonged to the Central Government.
Regulation 6 purportedly requires that a sanction is taken from the Central Government so as to effect a subsequent Transfer of Occupancy Rights.
According to the applicants, the Central Government did not sanction any transfer after the initial transfer of 1949.

Therefore, the applicants have been able to raise serious doubts about the petitioner's rights to receive compensation from the State Government without the consent of the Central Government or for that matter, for maintaining a writ petition especially in the absence of the Central Government.
The issues appear to go to the root of the matter.

11. The status of the Old Grant property and the overriding effect of the Government Grants Act,
1895 have been explained at length in the decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court in Dinshaw Shapoorjij Ankleswari's Case (supra).

In Repaka Bhyravamurthy's Case (supra), the High Court of Andhra Pradesh, inter alia, held that if any question arose that touched upon the issue of entitlement to the amount of compensation, the same might be considered by reason of an application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC.

12. Thus, it prima facie appears that the applicants ought to be added as respondents in the writ petition so that not only it could be ascertained whether a compensation for land acquisition can be paid to the petitioner without the consent of the Central Government, but also the question of maintainability can be determined after hearing the parties.
13. In view of the above and in the interest of justice, I allow the prayer of the applicants to be added as respondent parties.
The petitioner shall effect necessary amendment in the cause title.
